core_claim.quote: At this point, it will be clear that there are several scientific arguments to conclude that the reason why we have conscious visual sensations in Stage 4 is the recurrent interactions between visual areas. These sensations can be reported and manipulated because Stage 4 also includes the prefrontal and motor areas.

source.citation: Lamme VAF. How neuroscience will change our view on consciousness. Cognitive Neuroscience 1(3):204-220, 2010 (discussion paper; commentaries and response follow on pp. 220-240)

prediction.statement: When a person sees something they do not have to report or act on, the activity that marks the seeing is recurrent processing in the sensory areas; activity in the front and top of the brain (fronto-parietal areas), and the late P300 wave, come with reporting and using the stimulus, not with seeing it.

first_stated.passage: RP in Stage 3 is limited to visual areas, and hence cannot directly influence motor control and other functions necessary for direct report.

source.citation: Lamme VAF. How neuroscience will change our view on consciousness. Cognitive Neuroscience 1(3):204-220, 2010 (discussion paper; commentaries and response follow on pp. 220-240)

prediction.test_for: In a design where the stimulus is irrelevant to the task and nothing about it is reported, seen and unseen stimuli differ in sensory cortex but not reliably in fronto-parietal cortex or in the late positive wave; those later differences appear when the stimulus has to be reported or used.
prediction.test_against: In such a design, seeing is reliably accompanied by fronto-parietal activation or a late positive wave, or awareness is explained only when feedback from prefrontal cortex is kept while feedback within sensory cortex can be removed.

source.citation: Mashour GA, Roelfsema P, Changeux J-P, Dehaene S. Conscious processing and the global neuronal workspace hypothesis. Neuron 105(5):776-798, 2020
